entry.title: I Wrapped All My APIs Behind One Key and Started Selling Access (From Bangladesh)
entry.summary:
I maintain a handful of small APIs: a Grok chat bot, a Kimi chat API, an image generator, a photo enhancer, and a video downloader. Each had its own URL, its own auth (or none), and its own way of breaking at 2 AM. So I built a gateway. One endpoint, one API key, plan limits, and a dashboard. It's live at Rahad API Marketplace (Railway), and this is what I learned shipping it in about a day. One key (rk-...) for every backend: chat, image generation, photo enhancement, media download Plan limits that actually stop abuse: Free 100/day, Pro 5000/day, Unlimited 100k/day Usage is charged only when an upstream call succeeds — if my backend fails you, it shouldn't cost your quota A dashboard where you sign up, verify your email, and get a free key instantly Payments are the Bangladesh part of the story: no Stripe here, so Pro upgrades run through bKash with a manual transaction-ID approval flow. Ugly? A little. Working? Completely. When an upstream API fails (say it returns 401), my first version passed that straight through to the buyer. Their client then told them "unauthorized" — which sounds like their key is wrong. That's my bug wearing their error message. Fix: the gateway now translates any upstream failure into an honest 502 that names the backend, and only counts usage on success. Small change, much fairer billing. GET /v1/models doesn't pretend everything is fine. It probes the upstreams and reports real availability — if a backend is down, the endpoint says so instead of selling you a broken promise. Live: https://rahad-api-marketplace-production.up.railway.app
Free key: sign up, verify email, done — 100 requests/day, no card For those of you selling small APIs from countries without Stripe — how do you take money? Manual mobile-money approvals like mine, Paddle/Lemon Squeezy, or something else entirely? I'm genuinely deciding what to do next, and I'd rather learn from your scars than earn my own.

Freeze a Repo Contract Before Drafting Contributor Orientation
entry.summary: Generated contributor pages fail when a drafting model is allowed to invent owners, secrets, and license duties. Teams should freeze those facts in a repo contract before any orientation narrative is written at all. The model may explain existing contract entries in plain language, but it may not create new entries. A local checker can then reject drafts that cite missing identifiers or insert unsupported product claims. This split matters because onboarding text can look authoritative even when nobody has reviewed its hidden assumptions. A new contributor may treat a generated path owner as if it were a real review rule. The same reader may copy a generated secret location into a shell script before anyone notices the error. entry.title: Virtual threads are not dangerous; unbounded concurrency against a bounded dependency is.
entry.summary:
Oracle explicitly says virtual threads improve throughput rather than latency, should not be pooled, and scarce downstream resources should still have explicit concurrency limits. A database connection pool itself acts as such a limit. Imagine a Spring Boot payment API handling: 2,000 requests/sec 100 connections 20 ms 100 ÷ 0.020 ≈ 5,000 ops/sec 250 ms 100 ÷ 0.250 ≈ 400 ops/sec 2,000 requests/sec 1,600 requests/sec start waiting 10 seconds: 1,600 × 10 = 16,000 waiting requests 100 connections. The pool fills. DB slowdown → pool saturation → timeouts → retries → more load → worse saturation Virtual threads scale waiting.
They do not scale the database. bounded connection pools short timeouts controlled retries with jitter load shedding 10,000 virtual threads ≠ 10,000 database operations.
Java #SpringBoot #SoftwareArchitecture

entry.title: A Two-Commit Gate for a Messy Batch Module
entry.summary: A messy module should change only after today's outputs are frozen. A coding model may draft that freeze in a scratch repo. It should not ship a wide rewrite in the same commit. Land characterization tests before any production edit lands. Extract one pure function in the next commit. Reject the patch when production lines outgrow the test diff. Wide cleanups mix renames with real behavior changes. A quiet print tweak can break downstream parsers. Review time then goes to style, not to locked outputs. Side effects hide inside helper functions that look pure. Directory lists, file writes, and clocks are observations. Each one needs a golden assertion before a move. entry.title: What Researchers Actually Found When They Attacked Hardware Wallets
entry.summary: Every few months there's a headline saying hardware wallets get hacked. I wanted to know what the published attacks actually needed, so I went through them. Researchers have extracted keys from hardware wallets. But every documented case required physical access to the device, often with the case opened, or a unit that had been tampered with before the owner unboxed it. Nobody has done it remotely to someone using their wallet normally. At the Chaos Communication Congress in December 2018, three researchers presented Wallet.fail after spending months taking apart Trezor, Ledger and KeepKey devices. On the Trezor One they pulled the private key out. It only worked because no passphrase was set. A passphrase (the optional "25th word") closes that exact path. On the Ledger Nano S they comprom…

entry.title: The Payment Succeeded. The Response Never Arrived.
entry.summary:
A customer clicks Pay £100. The payment succeeds — but the response is lost. A robust design should: Generate the key once at the caller Reuse it for every retry Protect it with a DB unique constraint Store a request hash Persist the final response Pass the same key to the payment provider when supported The key lesson: A retry should repeat the request for the result — not repeat the business side effect.
Payments #SpringBoot #SoftwareArchitecture
